Indoor ventilation: classrooms, dormitories, offices, and cafeterias open 2–3 times daily for at least 30 minutes; in cold weather use intermittent airing. Daily cleaning of surfaces (floors, door handles, rails, desks, switches, dispensers, taps, bathrooms); use chlorine disinfectants for floors/walls at 250–500 mg/L and surfaces at 50–500 mg/L; 30-minute contact, then rinse. Foodware: boil utensils 15 minutes or use a dishwasher sterilizer; separate raw and cooked in kitchens. Emphasize hand hygiene; for suspected contaminated items, use higher-concentration disinfectants (e.g., 5,000 mg/L iodine or hypochlorite). Do not spray disinfectants indoors/outdoors; general waste need not be disinfected; report suspected cases and perform terminal disinfection under guidance.

articleSummary: Dengue virus (DENV) mutations across all four serotypes (DENV-1–DENV-4) are accelerating, with genomic changes in the Envelope (E) and NS1 proteins enhancing cell entry, immune escape, and enabling a heat-induced shift to a 'bumpy' surface that resists neutralization. Global dengue surge over the past year has disrupted traditional seasonality, with year-round transmission and expanding Aedes mosquito ranges into Europe and North America due to warming temperatures and urbanization. articleSummary: Escherichia coli bacteraemia at The University of Hong Kong-Shenzhen Hospital (2019–2023) involved 202 adults, with 19 in-hospital deaths (9.4%). The authors used Firth penalized logistic regression due to few deaths, with supporting ridge and LASSO analyses; wide CIs reflect sample size. Calibration slope ~1.13; decision-curve analysis shows net benefit at 5–50% thresholds. Internal validation included 5-fold cross-validation; temporal split (2019–2021 development, 2022–2023 testing) was exploratory due to only two deaths in the test set. articleSummary: 36-year-old woman in Qinghai, China, with intermittent right upper-quadrant pain and a history of hepatic hydatid disease due to Echinococcus granulosus. Echinococcus granulosus IgG serology was positive, but pancreatic lesion lacked classic hydatid imaging features. The team performed a right hepatectomy with common bile duct exploration and cholecystectomy to address biliary involvement and hepatic disease; the pancreatic lesion was evaluated intraoperatively by inspection/palpation, but intraoperative ultrasound was not used and pancreatic resection was avoided. Postoperative CT after one month showed no evident enlargement of the pancreatic cyst, though no pathological confirmation of the pancreatic lesion was obtained. The case underscores the diagnostic challenge of pancreatic echinococcosis as a rare entity and supports conservative management when pancreatic findings do not resemble hydatid disease.

articleHeadline: Dual-Genotype Protein Yields Broader ELISA for Hepatitis B preS1 Antibodies
articleSummary: HBV in China remains a leading driver of hepatocellular carcinoma due to persistent viral replication. Genotypic diversity complicates serology: genotypes B and C dominate East Asia, with >95% of Chinese HBV patients carrying B or C; B more common in the south and C in the north, and preS1 sequences vary by genotype. A Jilin University team built a dual-genotype ELISA using a fusion protein (B-C-preS1) spanning both B and C preS1 regions, enabling cross-genotype detection. Optimized assay conditions include coating 2 μg/mL, detection 1:200,000, PBS pH 8.0, overnight coating at 4°C, and HB2 as calibrator.

articleSummary: Brazil and global public health confront zoonoses—infectious diseases transmitted between animals and humans, caused by viruses, bacteria, parasites, or fungi. More than 200 zoonoses are known; about 60% of human infectious diseases and 75% of emerging infections originate in animals (WHO). Major zoonoses monitored in Brazil include dengue, Zika virus, chikungunya, leptospirosis, rabies, leishmaniasis, febre maculosa (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), toxoplasmosis, hantavirus, Chagas disease, and sporotrichosis. Risk depends on exposure and environment; living with healthy, vaccinated pets under veterinary care poses low risk and is not an inherent threat. Prevention requires an integrated One Health approach: vaccination, parasite control, hand hygiene after handling pets or cleaning litter, avoiding contact with unknown animals, treated water, clean food, protective measures in risk areas, and veterinary oversight. Seek medical care promptly for symptoms or suspected exposure; do not self-medicate. Responsible pet ownership protects both human and animal health.

The disease progresses rapidly: initial influenza-like symptoms (fever, fatigue, myalgia, cough) can within 2–3 days worsen to high fever, dyspnea, chest pain, and cyanosis, with imaging showing mediastinal widening, pleural effusion, or focal lesions. High-risk groups include livestock farmers, slaughterers, and workers in wool, cashmere, and fur processing; non-occupational exposure near markets or processing sites also poses risk. Prevention emphasizes risk recognition, avoiding exposure to dead animals and unverified products, use of protective masks, early medical consultation, and prompt, multi-drug antibiotic therapy under medical supervision.

articleHeadline: Ebola vaccine induces T cell cross-reactivity against Bundibugyo virus in humans
articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola virus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is the second largest Ebola outbreak globally, with over 6,000 confirmed cases and a 48% fatality rate; no BDBV-specific vaccine exists. Conserved glycoprotein epitopes underlie cross-reactivity. While clinical protection remains unproven, non-human primate data suggest T cells contribute to protection. Transmission occurs mainly through direct or indirect contact with infected birds or contaminated environments, including live bird markets; most cases are mild, but severe illness and fatalities have occurred, especially in people with underlying conditions. China reported 40 cases in 2025 and 31 cases between January and September 2026.

articleSummary: 263 million malaria cases and 597,000 deaths in 2023; Africa bears about 95% of the burden. articleSummary: Rabies risk to livestock in Amapá, Brazil, driven by hematophagous bats. Rabies is caused by Lyssavirus (Rhabdoviridae), endemic in South America; it is infectious, causes nervous signs, and has 100% mortality after symptoms appear. Prevention centers on vaccinating all susceptible livestock and investigating suspected bat attacks. On-farm vaccination is advised, and producers should notify Diagro when attacks occur. In focal and peripheral zones, vaccination becomes mandatory within a 12-km radius. People exposed should seek medical care; watch for bat roosts in caves, abandoned houses, and sheds to guide control actions.

articleSummary: Malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum uses melatonin signaling to regulate development in human hosts. USP researchers, with French collaborators, identified MT-PfSR1, a protein enabling recognition of melatonin and the parasite's response to human circadian cues, synchronizing growth within red blood cells. The parasite cycles roughly every 48 hours, with infected red blood cells rupturing at cycle end, releasing new parasites and driving fever outbreaks. In lab tests, the synthetic molecule AR34 activated MT-PfSR1 and inhibited parasite growth without binding human melatonin receptors, suggesting a potential drug target. Malaria is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes; symptoms include fever, extreme weakness, and in severe cases mental confusion, seizures, and breathing difficulties; without timely diagnosis, can be fatal. In Brazil, most cases occur in the Amazon region, including Amazonas, Pará, Acre, Rondônia, and Roraima. Further studies are needed to assess safety and efficacy in humans.

articleSummary: Democratic Republic of the Congo reports over 4,000 deaths from the ongoing Ebola outbreak, with more than 9,000 confirmed cases as of October 13, 2026. The outbreak began in Ituri province in northeastern DRC in mid-May 2026, though experts believe the virus may have circulated weeks or months earlier. It is the 17th Ebola outbreak in the DRC and has spread to seven provinces in the north and east. Limited health resources and armed-group activity hinder response, and healthcare and humanitarian workers face distrust from parts of local communities. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, for which no vaccine or specific treatment is currently approved. The World Health Organization announced an October vaccine trial to be deployed in DRC. Some frontline volunteers have received Ervebo, but its efficacy is against Zaire ebolavirus and does not confirm protection against Bundibugyo.
notes: Bundibugyoエボラウイルスによる第17次流行で、既承認ワクチン・治療薬が存在しない点が特に懸念材料。WHOによるワクチン治験開始が10月に予定されている。

articleHeadlineTranslated: DRC/Ebola: the epidemic is slowing, but its foci are moving (CDC Africa).
articleHeadline: RDC/Ebola : l'épidémie ralentit, mais ses foyers se déplacent (CDC Afrique)
articleSummary: Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of Congo shows signs of slowing, five months after its declaration, but new transmission foci complicate the response. CDC Africa Director Jean Kaseya said the two-week trend is downward, while the epidemic’s center of gravity shifts from Ituri province to neighboring North Kivu. Persistent gaps in surveillance and contact tracing continue to hinder interruption of transmission chains. Financial commitments for the response total about $3.045 billion, up from $1.656 billion in June, but only $962.66 million (31.6%) has been disbursed. Declared May 15, this outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, is the deadliest in the DRC and the second-largest globally after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. As of Oct 12, 2026, Congolese health authorities reported 9,144 confirmed cases and 4,410 deaths (case fatality rate 48.2%).

articleHeadline: TPHCM ghi nhận hơn 34.600 ca viêm hô hấp cấp trong một tuần
articleSummary: Ho Chi Minh City reports a surge in acute respiratory infections in week 40, totaling 34,664 cases, up more than 64% from the four-week average. Influenza remains a notable driver, with 151 influenza cases that week and 397 influenza cases reported since the start of the year. Laboratory typing shows influenza A predominance, with influenza A/H1N1 2009 accounting for 116 samples, about 77% of influenza-positive specimens that week. Health authorities (HCDC) maintain enhanced surveillance across 29 facilities and track community clusters to enable early detection. Weather transition and return to school are cited as factors facilitating transmission. Public health guidance urges hand hygiene, respiratory etiquette, masking when symptomatic, and medical care for fever, cough, sore throat, or nasal congestion, especially for the elderly and those with underlying conditions. Note: influenza A can cause rapid respiratory failure even without high fever.

articleHeadline: Ébola en RDC: el brote más mortífero en la historia del país
articleSummary: An Ebola outbreak declared mid-May in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has reached over 9,100 cases and 4,400 deaths, the deadliest in the country's history. Reports show 9,144 infections and 4,410 fatalities (case fatality rate 48.2%). In the last 24 hours, 79 new cases and 29 deaths were recorded. The National Public Health Institute (INSP) reports 899 patients hospitalized or in isolation and 2,418 recoveries. Seven provinces are affected, including North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele, Tshopo, and Ubangi-Sud (one additional province). The outbreak surpasses the 2018–2020 RDC event; projections suggest it could exceed West Africa's 2014–2016 crisis in Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone, which totaled 28,616 cases and 11,325 deaths, per WHO.

articleHeadlineTranslated: RSV high-incidence season arrives as new long-acting preventive monoclonal antibody lands in Beijing
articleHeadline: 呼吸道合胞病毒高发季来临，新型长效预防单抗落地北京 -- 新京报
articleSummary: As of 2026-10-14, northern China has entered the RSV high-incidence season, with Beijing approving and rolling out an imported long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody administered in a fixed dose (weight-independent) for infants, and several Beijing medical institutions opening vaccination appointments. RSV is the leading cause of infant respiratory infections; nearly all children are infected by age two, and infections in infants under one year can be severe, leading to hospitalization, pneumonia, bronchiolitis, and potentially respiratory failure. Long-term risks include reduced lung function and about a threefold increase in later wheeze and asthma. Public awareness gaps persist; many parents underestimate RSV and its severity. There is no specific antiviral therapy, so prevention is key. WHO regards RSV monoclonal antibodies as important preventive tools. China already has several long-acting RSV monoclonals approved for newborns/young infants; Beijing’s Chaoyang District CDC notes the burden and directs families to use 京通 or 首都疫苗服务APP to locate and book pilot sites.
notes: 季節性RSVの流行と新規予防薬（モノクローナル抗体）の展開に関する通常の医療ニュースであり、感染症危機管理上のシグナルには該当しない。

articleHeadline: 肯尼亞出現第二宗伊波拉個案　患者為首宗個案親屬
articleSummary: As of 14 October 2026, Kenya reports a second locally acquired Bundibugyo ebolavirus case. The patient is a 39-year-old man, a relative of the first confirmed case, who developed fever, fatigue and joint pains. He was identified as a close contact, is in isolation under medical surveillance, and has been transferred to a designated treatment center; authorities are tracing contacts, including healthcare workers. Officials say the two cases are related and there is no evidence of broader community transmission. The first case was an imported Ebola patient from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a Kenyan citizen who had lived in DRC for seven years, who arrived in Nairobi and subsequently died. For the first case, 128 contacts were identified: 15 not traced, 108 isolated domestically, and 5 who had traveled abroad; relevant countries and regions have been notified.

articleHeadline: DR Congo: Cholera Cases Spike Amid Fight Against Ebola
articleSummary: Cholera in the Democratic Republic of Congo has over 125,000 suspected cases and 3,644 deaths from January 2025 to late September 2026, with South Kivu, North Kivu and Haut-Katanga hosting about 60% of cases. Four new health zones are affected (three in Tshuapa, one in South Kivu) amid security challenges, limited access in Kibua and Masisi, and contamination from wells and rainfall. Response includes four water-chlorination sites in North Kivu, disinfecting about 4,000 households and 5,900 latrines in Tanganyika, and cross-border vaccination planning with the Republic of Congo; reactive campaigns continue in Mulungu and Shabunda. Ebola, caused by Bundibugyo strain, totals 9,066 cases and 4,381 deaths (CFR 48.3%) across seven provinces and 65 health zones, with 2,389 recoveries. Isiro Ebola treatment centre is expanded; WHO delivered additional medical supplies. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August; Kenya reported an imported fatal case linked to travel from DRC, with a possible second case.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Regions across the country are gradually entering the autumn-winter influenza season: how should parents respond scientifically?
articleHeadline: 各地陆续进入秋冬流感流行季 家长如何科学应对？ _光明网
articleSummary: As of 2026-10-15, China enters autumn–winter influenza season, with children and adolescents at highest risk. In Shanghai, influenza A spreads rapidly and mutates, while influenza B is more common among youths. Flu onset is abrupt with high fever and systemic symptoms; colds are milder with local symptoms. Age-specific features: 0–3 years may have irritability or poor feeding; 3–6 years with fever and cough; 6+ resemble adults with high fever and malaise. Antivirals work best within 24–48 hours: oseltamivir for children 2 weeks and older; baloxavir marboxil for 1 year and older; both prescription-only. Monitor after dosing and seek urgent care if fever persists or if signs include drowsiness, seizures, rapid breathing, blue lips, fever >3 days, or no urination >8 hours. Vaccination from 6 months is the most effective preventive measure and remains protective even if given later in autumn–winter. Source: Shanghai Children’s Hospital and Xinhua News Agency.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Understanding the Plague, an Age-Old Disease That Still Requires Vigilance.
articleHeadline: Mengenal Pes, Penyakit Lama yang Masih Perlu Diwaspadai
articleSummary: Plague (Yersinia pestis) remains a vigilance concern. While rumors about a Russian lab incident circulated, Russia’s government attributed deaths to pneumonia with an unconfirmed cause, and Indonesian experts caution against speculative links. In Indonesia, there is no confirmed human plague outbreak; however, Y. pestis persists in wild rodents, notably rats, maintaining a potential reservoir. Plague transmission is primarily via fleas from infected rodents, direct contact with infected animal fluids, or droplets. Pneumonic plague, the most severe form, affects the lungs and can spread between animals and humans, and among people through droplets. The article emphasizes an ongoing, latent risk of plague and urges cautious interpretation of information, while noting the need for vigilance regarding any outbreaks in the region, including Indonesia. Published date: 2026-10-15.

articleHeadline: Macau tightens screening after unexplained pneumonia death in Russia
articleSummary: Macau tightened border health screening after a Russia-based researcher died of pneumonia of unknown cause in Irkutsk region on Oct. 5; immediate public health risk remains low. Macau's Health Bureau (SSM) requires travellers who visited Irkutsk within 14 days of entry to report travel history and undergo screening, including voluntary declarations at major crossings and enhanced fever checks. Suspected cases of pneumonia of unknown cause will be transferred to Conde de São Januário Hospital for assessment and testing; medical institutions will be alerted to report unexplained pneumonia in patients with Irkutsk exposure within 14 days of symptom onset. Rospotrebnadzor announced the death and denied pneumonic plague or lab accident; WHO information notes no plague and no sustained transmission, though the pathogen is unidentified. Hong Kong is adding checks for arrivals from Russia; CHP says immediate risk is low; WHO will monitor and SSM will adjust precautions as needed. Residents with fever, cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath after travel should seek medical care and disclose travel history.
notes: 事件発生地はロシア・イルクーツク州であり、対象国リストに含まれないため verified_locations は空。マカオ・香港は渡航者スクリーニング強化の対応を取っているのみで、発生地ではないため除外。WHOはペスト及び持続的ヒト-ヒト感染を否定しているが、病原体は未特定であり続報を要する。

articleHeadline: Kasus DBD Jakarta Naik, Jaksel Catat 1.314 Kasus hingga September
articleSummary: Dengue fever (DBD) in Jakarta is rising, with Jakarta Selatan reporting 1,314 cases through September 2026 (IR 56.55). The DKI Jakarta Health Office states the increase aligns with seasonal climate patterns and is being monitored by comparing monthly totals and year-on-year data to assess control. Reports of five dengue deaths in Jakarta Timur through August are not reflected in the Health Office’s current data, which shows no deaths yet, pending source verification. Officials urge intensified vector control and public education, including routine, synchronized 3M Plus mosquito-source elimination at least weekly and the Satu Rumah Satu Jumantik program. DPRD Jakarta calls for stronger surveillance, facility readiness (Puskesmas and RSUD in South Jakarta), and fogging as indicated. Ongoing monitoring aims to ensure rapid, adequate care and prevent further spread across the capital.
